title.rendered: Best AI image generators in 2026: prices and commercial rights

content.raw:
The best AI image generator in 2026 depends on the job. Midjourney suits stylised art, OpenAI's GPT Image and Google's Nano Banana models suit text-heavy graphics and chat-based editing, FLUX suits teams that want to self-host, and Adobe Firefly suits brands that want legal cover. Below we compare all five on quality, editing, API access, price and commercial-use terms, using vendor pages checked on 4 October 2026.

Key takeaways

  • Every vendor here lets you use outputs commercially, but the fine print differs: Midjourney requires a Pro or Mega plan if your company earns more than $1 million a year, and the free FLUX.2 [dev] weights are for non-commercial use only.
  • Adobe says outputs from its own Firefly models are safe for commercial use and offers IP indemnification to eligible enterprise customers. OpenAI and Google offer indemnities through business contracts and Google Cloud.
  • Google has shut down Imagen in the Gemini API; its image models are now the Nano Banana line, led by Nano Banana 2 (Gemini 3.1 Flash Image) and Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro Image).
  • Provenance marking is now standard: Google stamps every Gemini API image with SynthID, OpenAI adds both C2PA Content Credentials and SynthID, and Adobe attaches Content Credentials.

How we compared the generators

We did not rank on taste alone. Each tool was judged on seven criteria using the vendor's own pricing pages, documentation, licence files and terms: image quality and style; text rendering; editing (references, multi-turn edits); API access; price; commercial rights and indemnity (who owns outputs and whether the vendor will defend you against an IP claim); and open weights for self-hosting.

Prices below are the US-dollar list prices shown on vendor pages on 4 October 2026. Readers in India and elsewhere may see local-currency prices, such as rupees, and amounts vary by country.

This article summarises vendor terms for comparison only. It is not legal advice; confirm licensing questions with a qualified professional before you rely on them.

Midjourney: best for art direction and mood

Midjourney's current default is V8.2, which became the default on 24 July 2026, according to Midjourney's version documentation. It focuses on aesthetics and personalisation and adds a new Edit Model that replaces Omni Reference, Character Reference and Retexture. V8.1, released in April, added native 2K "HD" images.

Price and plans

Midjourney sells four subscriptions, according to its plan comparison page: Basic at $10 a month, Standard at $30, Pro at $60 and Mega at $120, with a 20% discount for annual billing. Basic includes 3.3 hours of fast GPU time a month; Standard and above add unlimited "Relax" image generation.

Commercial rights and privacy

Midjourney's terms of service (effective 27 May 2026) say you own the assets you create to the fullest extent the law allows, with an important exception: a company, or an employee of a company, with more than $1,000,000 a year in revenue must be on Pro or Mega to own its assets.

By default your images are publicly viewable and remixable, and you grant Midjourney a broad licence to prompts and outputs. Stealth mode, which keeps work off the public site, is only available on Pro and Mega, and even then anything you create in a public Discord channel stays visible. The terms also ask you to indemnify Midjourney against third-party claims, not the other way round.

Who it suits: designers, agencies and creators who care most about look and feel and will do final layout and type elsewhere. Businesses above the revenue line should budget for Pro.

OpenAI GPT Image: best for instructions, text and editing in chat

OpenAI's API now offers two current image models, gpt-image-2.5-sunburst and gpt-image-2.5-flare. According to OpenAI's image generation guide, Sunburst is meant for work where editing precision matters most, while Flare targets fast, high-quality everyday generation. Both work through the Image API or as a tool in the Responses API.

OpenAI's documentation admits that complex prompts can take up to two minutes and that text rendering can still struggle with precise placement.

Price

Both GPT Image 2.5 models share the same token rates: $8 per million image input tokens, $30 per million image output tokens and $5 per million text input tokens. Cost per picture therefore depends on size and quality setting.

In the consumer app, the ChatGPT pricing page lists limited image creation on the free plan, more on Go ($8 a month) and "more complex and accurate" image creation on Plus ($20 a month). Pro, from $100 a month, advertises unlimited and faster image creation.

Commercial rights

OpenAI's Terms of Use (effective 1 January 2026) say that, as between you and OpenAI, you own the output, and OpenAI assigns to you whatever rights it has in it. The terms warn that other users may receive similar output. For businesses, OpenAI's Services Agreement includes an indemnity in which OpenAI agrees to defend customers against third-party claims that its services infringe IP rights, subject to listed exclusions such as customer content and modifications.

On provenance, OpenAI's help centre says supported images from ChatGPT, Codex and the API carry both C2PA metadata and a SynthID watermark, and anyone can check a file at openai.com/verify.

Who it suits: marketers, product teams and founders who want to describe an edit in plain language, iterate inside a chat, or wire image generation into an app. Our OpenAI jobs page lists its open roles.

Google Nano Banana: best value API and strongest on world knowledge

If you are still searching for "Imagen", note that Google has retired it. The Gemini API image generation docs say Imagen models are shut down and that Nano Banana models should be used for all image generation. The current line-up:

  • Nano Banana 2 (Gemini 3.1 Flash Image): Google's generalist model, which it says offers 4K generation, world knowledge, reliable text rendering and strong multi-reference consistency.
  • Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro Image): the premium model for complex tasks, localisation and brand consistency.
  • Nano Banana 2 Lite (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite Image): the fastest and cheapest, not optimised for multiple references or multi-turn editing.

Price

Google's Gemini API pricing works out to about $0.067 per 1K (1024x1024) image and $0.151 per 4K image on Nano Banana 2, about $0.134 per image up to 2K on Nano Banana Pro, and about $0.034 per 1K image on Nano Banana 2 Lite. Image models are not available on the free API tier, and Google states that paid-tier content is not used to improve its products.

Commercial rights and watermarking

The Gemini API terms say Google won't claim ownership of generated content, while reserving the right to generate the same or similar content for others. Every image includes a SynthID watermark, which Google DeepMind describes as an imperceptible signal its tools can detect. For an indemnity, Google Cloud's list of generative AI indemnified services covers its enterprise agent platform API (formerly Vertex AI) when used with generally available Gemini, Imagen and Veo models.

Who it suits: developers who need many images at low cost, and teams producing infographics, diagrams or localised marketing where text and real-world accuracy matter.

FLUX by Black Forest Labs: best for self-hosting and custom models

Black Forest Labs (BFL) is the one vendor here that publishes model weights. Its pricing page lists the FLUX.2 family ([klein] 4B and 9B, [flex], [pro] and [max]) alongside FLUX 3 Image, Video and Action. FLUX 3, announced on 23 July 2026 and in early access, is trained on images, video and audio together; BFL says it handles complex prompts and text much better than earlier FLUX versions.

The hosted API is pay as you go with "no subscriptions, no seat fees". Example rates on the page range from $0.024 to $0.048 per image depending on model and resolution.

The licence trap: dev is not free for business

According to the FLUX.2 GitHub repository, only FLUX.2 [klein] 4B (and its base variant) is released under the permissive Apache 2.0 licence. FLUX.2 [dev] and the [klein] 9B models use the FLUX Non-Commercial License v2.1, which allows the weights only for non-commercial purposes. It says revenue-generating use, or use that affects end users, is not non-commercial.

There is a nuance. The same licence says BFL claims no ownership of outputs and that you may use outputs for any purpose, including commercial ones, except to train a competing model. It also requires content filtering or human review, and asks you to indemnify BFL. Running [dev] in production for a business still needs a paid licence. BFL's licensing page offers Builder (klein models, 10,000 images a month, one domain), Platform (adds FLUX.2 [dev], 100,000 images a month, aimed at SaaS products), Professional (for agencies, first three clients included) and Enterprise tiers.

Who it suits: engineering teams that want to fine-tune on their own product photos or brand style, keep data on their own servers, or control cost at volume. New image tools also show up on our launches page.

Adobe Firefly: best for commercial safety and design workflows

Adobe's pitch is about risk. Its Firefly plans page says outputs from Adobe Firefly models are safe for commercial use because they are trained on licensed and public-domain content, and that eligible enterprise customers can receive IP indemnification for select Firefly outputs. Adobe also attaches Content Credentials automatically, and its generative AI user guidelines forbid users from removing or altering them.

One caveat: Firefly now also hosts partner models, including GPT Image, Gemini (Nano Banana) and FLUX. Adobe's own FAQ says you are responsible for deciding whether partner-model output is appropriate for your project, so the commercial-safety promise applies to Adobe's own models, not every model inside the app.

Price

The plans page lists a free tier with limited daily generations, then Firefly Standard at $9.99 a month (2,000 generative credits), Pro at $19.99 (4,000 credits), Pro Plus at $49.99 (10,000 credits) and Premium at $199.99 (50,000 credits). All paid plans include unlimited standard image generations; credits are spent on video, audio and partner-model outputs.

Who it suits: in-house brand teams, agencies with large clients and anyone already working in Adobe's apps.

Can you copyright AI-generated images?

Owning an output under a vendor's terms is not the same as holding copyright in it. In January 2025 the US Copyright Office concluded that AI outputs can be protected only where a human author has determined sufficient expressive elements, for example through creative arrangement or modification. It said that merely providing prompts is not enough, though using AI as an assistive tool does not bar protection. Other countries apply their own rules, so have a designer refine important brand assets such as logos.

Bottom line: which AI image generator to use for what

  • Mood boards, concept art, editorial illustration: Midjourney, on Pro if your company passes $1 million in revenue or needs privacy.
  • Social graphics, ads with copy, quick edits from a chat: ChatGPT with GPT Image 2.5, or Gemini with Nano Banana 2.
  • High-volume API work on a budget: Nano Banana 2 Lite or FLUX.2 via the BFL API.
  • Self-hosting and fine-tuning: FLUX.2 [klein] 4B for Apache 2.0 freedom, or a paid BFL licence for [dev].
  • Enterprise campaigns where legal review is strict: Adobe Firefly's own models, ideally on an enterprise plan with indemnity.

Many teams will use two tools: one for ideas and one for production-safe output. Follow our AI news coverage for model updates, and see AI and ML jobs if you want to work on these systems.

FAQ

Which AI image generator is best for commercial use?

Adobe Firefly is the most conservative choice because Adobe trains its own models on licensed and public-domain content and offers IP indemnification to eligible enterprise customers. OpenAI and Google also let you use outputs commercially and offer indemnities through business and cloud contracts.

Can I use Midjourney images commercially on the Basic plan?

Yes, if you are an individual or a company with under $1 million in annual revenue. Larger companies and their employees must subscribe to Pro or Mega to own their assets, according to Midjourney's terms.

Is FLUX free for commercial use?

Only partly. FLUX.2 [klein] 4B is Apache 2.0. FLUX.2 [dev] and [klein] 9B weights are non-commercial, though the licence lets you use their outputs commercially. Production business use of [dev] needs a paid BFL licence.

How can I tell if an image was made with AI?

Check for Content Credentials (C2PA metadata) or a SynthID watermark. OpenAI offers a checker at openai.com/verify. A missing label does not prove an image is human-made.
